Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) stock rebounded 7.79% on Monday after the chipmaker's shares experienced a rough couple of days last week. The rally of AMD stock came alongside praise from one of Wall Street's top analysts. Five-star Bernstein analyst Mark Newman reiterated a Buy rating and a $650 price target for AMD stock, implying a possible 43.74% upside.

Newman came out to support AMD after the company was targeted in a short report last week. Hunterbrook was behind this report and claimed that AMD has continued to provide support for GPUs that belong to blacklisted Chinese companies. However, AMD claimed that this report misrepresented its practices. While investors were rattled by that report, a continued bullish stance from a top Wall Street analyst appears to have boosted morale today.

Should Investors Trust Newman on AMD?

Newman is a highly-ranked analyst on TipRanks, placing 209 out of 12,607 Wall Street analysts. He is also ranked 1,112 out of 37,861 experts on the platform. His Success Rate is 59%, with 42 out of 71 ratings generating a profit. The analyst also has an Average Return of 37.4% per rating.

Newman is an analyst that is heavily focused on the computer hardware sector. Other stocks in this sector that he covers include Nvidia (NVDA), Intel (INTC), Broadcom (AVGO), SanDisk (SNDK), Western Digital (WDC), and Seagate (STX).

What Other News Is Affecting AMD Stock Today?

In a major surprise, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang will return as the company's CEO. He resigned earlier this month following allegations of extramarital affairs, including one affair with a possible Chinese spy, as reported by TipRanks. His departure shocked the tech sector, putting pressure on AI stocks.

With Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO, AI and tech stocks were on the rise today. AMD was among them, as the rival semiconductor company extends a 98.16% year-to-date rally. Investors will also note that shares of AMD have gained 97.35% over the past 12 months.

Is AMD Stock a Buy, Sell, or Hold?

Investing.com -- Advanced Micro Devices Inc (NASDAQ:AMD) filed a Form S-3 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday to register up to 336,934,324 shares of common stock for potential future resale by existing shareholders and strategic partners. The filing accommodates stock-based consideration from recent acquisitions alongside massive performance-linked warrants held by OpenAI (NASDAQ:OAI) and Meta Platforms Inc (NASDAQ:META), though AMD itself is not selling any shares and will receive no proceeds from the transactions.

The overwhelming majority of the registered stock stems from two major commercial arrangements, with OpenAI and Meta each eligible to acquire and resell up to 160 million shares at an exercise price of $0.01 per share. Neither warrant is currently exercisable, and the underlying shares will only vest in tranches tied to substantial hardware procurement milestones and stock-price appreciation.

For both OpenAI and Meta, initial share vesting requires the delivery or shipment of an initial one gigawatt equivalent of AMD Instinct GPU products, including AMD Instinct MI450 Series hardware for OpenAI. Full vesting of the 160 million shares for each partner is contingent upon cumulative purchases reaching six gigawatts, alongside the fulfillment of technical conditions and AMD share-price targets that escalate to $600 per share for the final tranche.

Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), an AI and CPU chips provider, closed at $453.46, up 6.85%. Shares rose after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and investors are watching AI-chip sentiment and conference commentary.
Trading volume reached 53.0M shares, coming in about 93% above its three-month average of 27.5M shares.

How the markets moved today

S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) closed at 7,237, up 4.73%, while Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) closed at 24,090, up 6.51%. Among semiconductors and semiconductor equipment peers, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) closed at $165.05, up 31.48%, and Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) closed at $59.66, up 16.34%, highlighting a broad AI-chip rebound.

What this means for investors

AMD was one of the many stocks that benefited from the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO. This stands in contrast to what happened Friday when AMD stock plunged on a short-seller report. The report alleged that some AMD server firmware fell into the hands of a blacklisted Chinese company.

By today, that report appeared to be forgotten. Although AMD is a major competitor to Nvidia in the data center space, it benefits indirectly as Huang's return breathes new life into the AI trade and brings stability to the semiconductor sector.

Fortunately, AMD has made technical progress to the point that it may benefit directly as well. Many industry analysts believe that AMD's MI450 series GPU (along with the MI455X Helios rack) has, at least on paper, caught up to Nvidia's latest release, the Vera Rubin.

Admittedly, at a P/E ratio of 98, the tech stock remains far more expensive than Nvidia, which, even with its gains today, trades at just 18 times earnings. However, analysts forecast that AMD's revenue will grow at 51% annually this year, then rise to 84% in 2027.

Amid a reinvigorated AI trade, such growth gives investors all the more reason to take a closer look at AMD stock.

Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, used the November 20 episode of his podcast, The Real Eisman Playbook, to argue that the AI market has changed: "Without Nvidia backstopping the AI stack, AI is no longer one trade. And that's why stock picking is back, and valuation is back."

Shutterstock

Three days later, the board of NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, and the stock rose 32.36% in today's session. Does his return undo Eisman's thesis? The price data suggests the split he described had already happened.

NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Why Eisman Says NVIDIA Held the AI Trade Together

Eisman's argument centers on circular financing. He said Huang took equity stakes in, or lent money to, companies including Anthropic, OpenAI, CoreWeave and Nebius Group, and those companies then used the money to buy NVIDIA chips. "He created, I think, a virtual vertical holding company," Eisman said. When one balance sheet supports the whole network, having any AI stock means having a piece of the same machine. Once that support passes, Eisman said, the companies "need to be evaluated on their own merits and not as part of a larger whole."

Steve Eisman Said AI Was "No Longer One Trade." Huang Is Back, but Alphabet and CoreWeave Still Show the Split ©Nickel_Bell from Getty Images and Изображения пользователя Axel Makhalov via Canva
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom and CoreWeave fell 12% to 14% on Friday, while Alphabet fell 2.6%.

Steve Eisman said Jensen Huang's exit would end NVIDIA's backing of its own customers, including CoreWeave and Nebius, before the board reinstated Huang on Nov. 23.

Alphabet funds its buildout on its own name. CoreWeave built on borrowed money.

AI stocks stopped trading as one group on Friday, and they split by who pays for what.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) fell 14%, AMD 13% and Broadcom 12%. CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) also fell 12% and now sits more than 70% below its peak. Alphabet (GOOG) fell 2.6%. Nebius (NBIS:NASDAQ) and Dell Technologies (DELL:NYSE) face the same funding question as CoreWeave: one as a fellow neocloud, the other as its server supplier.

Under Huang, NVIDIA put $2 billion into CoreWeave in January and $2 billion into Nebius in March. Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, described it on The Real Eisman Playbook:

"Essentially, he gave them money, and they used that money to buy his chips. He created, I think, a virtual vertical holding company."

Huang's resignation ended that, Eisman said before the board reinstated Huang on Nov. 23: "Without Nvidia backstopping the AI stack, AI is no longer one trade."

Alphabet Raises Money on Its Own Name

Alphabet never needed NVIDIA's money. Free cash flow stayed at $60 billion or more every year through 2025, even as capex climbed.

GOOG Free Cash Flow: 2021-2025 (TIKR)

2026 broke that pattern. Alphabet expects $195 billion to $205 billion of capex this year, more than double 2025's $91.4 billion. Free cash flow fell to $19.7 billion over the 12 months to September, and in June Alphabet announced plans to raise $80 billion from stock sales.

That means dilution, but Alphabet raises the money on its own name, with a $561 billion Google Cloud backlog behind it.

CoreWeave Has to Stand on Its Own Now

CoreWeave runs the other way. It built its data centers on borrowed money, and the debt piled up fast.

CRWV Total Debt: 2023-2025 (TIKR)

That's nearly 15 times as much debt in two years. Eisman says companies like it now "need to be evaluated on their own merits and not as part of a larger whole."

Nebius's third-quarter revenue rose to $980.8 million from $146.1 million a year earlier. But it now expects about $27 billion of capex this year and $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027, with prepayments and financing against customer contracts covering 75% to 85% of next year's bill.

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) delivered a blockbuster Q3 FY2026 report, but the broader pullback in semiconductor stocks is overshadowing its strong results. Revenue reached $13.4 billion, up 45% year-over-year. Growth was driven by record Data Center revenue of $8.5 billion, up 97% year-over-year on strong demand for EPYC processors and Instinct graphics processing units (GPUs). Looking ahead, management also guided Q4 2026 revenue to about $17 billion.

Despite the recent sector-wide sell-off, I remain bullish on AMD stock and maintain a Buy rating, given its accelerating data center scale and management's positive outlook for Q4.

For context, AMD designs and sells computer chip processors that power products like servers and personal computers (PCs).

AMD Data Center Revenue

On the Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CEO Lisa Su stated the company forecasts Data Center segment revenue to be "more than 80% of our total revenue in 2027." Meanwhile, Q3 revenue was reported at $13.4 billion, up 45% year-over-year, and guidance was set at $17 billion for Q4 FY2026. Adding the first nine months' revenue of $35 billion to the $17 billion expected in Q4 puts the company on track for roughly $52 billion in FY2026.

Looking ahead, the company expects total revenue to grow more than 80% in 2027, with Data Center revenue making up more than 80% of that. This implies revenue of at least $93.6 billion, including roughly $74.9 billion from data centers. To put that figure in perspective, Nvidia (NVDA) reported $107.6 billion in data center revenue in a single quarter, Q3 FY2027.

AMD isn't in the same league as Nvidia, but it is trending upward and comes without all of the risks Nvidia faces going into 2027. The company could capture market share if Nvidia loses momentum due to Jensen Huang's departure.

To support management guidance on total revenue, Su mentioned that customers such as Anthropic (ANT) and Meta (META) brought their first Helios racks online this quarter and are already running their latest models on them. The company also pointed to Meta's Muse, a consumer agentic artificial intelligence (AI) product, as an example of agentic AI growth lifting demand for its EPYC server central processing units (CPUs). This, in turn, supports the expectation that total revenue will grow as enterprise and consumer agentic AI usage increases. Data center and server refresh revenue are the underlying drivers for my bull case on AMD.
